# Smooth threshold depth has no nontrivial lattice source interpolation

This is an independent proof and audit of the new outward-threshold smoothing mechanism proposed by Topological. It concerns the actual smoothed body-only objective. It does not assert parity separation for the unsmoothed objective, and does not by itself prove OC.

## 1. Exact model and local hypotheses

Let \(C\) be convex, let \(P\) be its finite sampled integer base, and let all sampled fibers have positive \(d\)-volume, where \(d\geq1\). Write \(\mu=\sum_{z\in P}\delta_z\otimes 1_{K_z}\,dx\). Let \(f\) be continuous and concave on \(C\). Let \(\Gamma\) be a norm on continuous covectors, independent of the cap's base normal.

Fix \(\epsilon\geq0,\delta>0\). Choose a smooth probability density \(\psi\) supported on \([-1,0]\), positive on \((-1,0)\), and let \(\Psi\) be its cumulative distribution function. For \(u\ne0\), define

\[
T(a,u,b)=\int\Psi\!\left(\frac{a\cdot z+u\cdot x-b}{\delta\Gamma(u)}\right)\,d\mu(z,x),
\qquad b_{a,u}(Y)=a\cdot p+u\cdot y-\epsilon f(Y)\Gamma(u).
\]

The smoothed depth is the infimum of \(T(a,u,b_{a,u}(Y))\) over all nonvertical normals, together with the original closed pure-base cap masses. All masses here are raw; division by the common positive total mass changes none of the arguments.

Let \(Q\) be the attained maximum over \(S\). Assume every maximizing mark has an attained nonvertical minimizing cap for which

\[
S(a,u,b):=\int\frac{\psi((a\cdot z+u\cdot x-b)/(\delta\Gamma(u)))}{\delta\Gamma(u)}\,d\mu>0.
\tag{1}
\]

Only positivity at the cap ultimately used is required; no global positive derivative or uniqueness of minimizing normals is assumed.

## 2. Convex depth regions

For fixed \((a,u)\), \(b\mapsto T(a,u,b)\) is continuous and nonincreasing, tending from the total mass to zero. Thus for \(0<Q<\mu(S)\) its \(Q\)-superlevel is a closed initial interval \((-\infty,c_Q(a,u)]\). The mark condition is exactly

\[
a\cdot p+u\cdot y-\epsilon f(Y)\Gamma(u)\leq c_Q(a,u).
\]

This is a convex sublevel constraint because \(f\) is concave. The unchanged closed pure-base tails give closed affine constraints in precisely the same way. Therefore the depth-at-least-\(Q\) region in \(C\) is convex.

In particular any convex combination of maximizing mixed-integer marks whose base is integer is again a maximizing mark.

## 3. Propagation of one attained cap along an arbitrary source interpolation

Suppose \(Y=\sum_{i=1}^r t_iY_i\), with all \(t_i>0\), \(\sum t_i=1\), where each \(Y_i\) is maximizing and the base of \(Y\) is integer. Take an attained cap at \(Y\) satisfying (1), and put \(b=b_{a,u}(Y)\), \(b_i=b_{a,u}(Y_i)\). Then

\[
T(a,u,b)=Q,\qquad T(a,u,b_i)\geq Q.
\tag{2}
\]

Differentiating under the integral gives \(\partial_b T(a,u,b)=-S(a,u,b)<0\). The derivative is continuous, so the tail is strictly decreasing on a neighborhood of \(b\). Monotonicity outside that neighborhood then implies

\[
T(a,u,b_i)\geq T(a,u,b)\ \Longrightarrow\ b_i\leq b.
\tag{3}
\]

This implication uses only local strict decrease at \(b\), not strict decrease at all thresholds. Concavity of \(f\) gives

\[
b\leq\sum_i t_i b_i.
\tag{4}
\]

Combining (3) and (4) forces every \(b_i=b\). The very same full ambient cap is therefore minimizing at every \(Y_i\). There is no source-dependent threshold, cap replacement, or lost boundary mass in this propagation.

## 4. Exact smooth base-normal stationarity

At a fixed source \(Y_i=(p_i,y_i)\), vary the base normal \(a\) to \(a+t v\), leaving \(u\) fixed. Its through-source threshold changes from \(b\) to \(b+t\,v\cdot p_i\). Neither \(\delta\Gamma(u)\) nor \(\epsilon f(Y_i)\Gamma(u)\) changes.

The derivative of this actual cap mass at \(t=0\) is

\[
\int \frac{\psi((a\cdot z+u\cdot x-b)/(\delta\Gamma(u)))}{\delta\Gamma(u)}
\,v\cdot(z-p_i)\,d\mu.
\tag{5}
\]

The integrand derivative is bounded on the compact support, so differentiation under the integral is justified. Since the cap is a global minimizing normal at \(Y_i\), (5) vanishes for every signed \(v\in\mathbb R^n\). Hence

\[
p_i=\frac{\displaystyle\int z\,\psi((a\cdot z+u\cdot x-b)/(\delta\Gamma(u)))\,d\mu}
{\displaystyle\int\psi((a\cdot z+u\cdot x-b)/(\delta\Gamma(u)))\,d\mu}.
\tag{6}
\]

Its denominator is positive by (1), and the right side is independent of \(i\). All source bases participating in the interpolation are therefore identical.

## 5. Lattice consequences

Let \(I\) be the set of maximizing integer bases. There is no integer convex combination of distinct bases in \(I\) with positive coefficients. More precisely, every such combination would give the maximizing mark of Section 3, contradicting (6).

Consequently:

1. \(I=\operatorname{conv}(I)\cap\mathbb Z^n\).
2. Every point of \(I\) is a vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(I)\); this hull has no other lattice points, including on its faces.
3. Two different bases in \(I\) cannot have the same parity, because their midpoint would be integer. Therefore \(|I|\leq2^n\).

For \(n=0\) the base set is a singleton, as expected. The proof is valid when the affine rank of \(I\) is smaller than \(n\); no unimodular reduction is needed. It does not assert that the limiting unsmoothed deepest set retains any of these strict properties.

## 6. Verification of the local hypotheses for small outward H smoothing

For the body-tied profile \(f_H\) and covariance norm, the compact positive-fiber H model supplies uniform slab-area bounds and uniform comparison

\[
0\leq b_{\epsilon,\delta}(Y)-b_\epsilon^H(Y)\leq C\delta,
\qquad
0\leq b_\epsilon^H(Y)-b_0(Y)\leq C\epsilon.
\]

The first inequality is immediate from the outward kernel: \(\Psi(s)\geq1_{\{s\geq0\}}\), with the difference supported on a slab of width \(\delta\Gamma(u)\). The estimates are uniform over all base tilts. Since original maximal depth has a positive uniform lower bound, sufficiently small \(\epsilon,\delta\) force every new maximizing mark into the old uniform own-interior core. Taking them smaller again puts the entire kernel slab around every through-source buffered cut inside a fixed own ball, after continuous-normal normalization.

On a fixed subinterval of \((-1,0)\), \(\psi\) has a positive lower bound. Integrating its corresponding subslab through that own ball proves (1), uniformly. This remains true in \(d=1\), where each own cross section has counting coarea \(1/|u|\).

Pure-base caps cannot attain the depth at such a source: tilt a pure-base minimizer by a sufficiently small nonzero continuous component. For large finite base-to-continuous ratio, all nonzero base drifts retain their old full/empty status. On zero-drift bases the smooth integrand is at most one, while the source's own core supplies positive mass where it is strictly below one. The resulting cap has strictly smaller mass than the closed pure-base cap.

Finally the finite clipping/minimum-norm reduction remains exact. After normalizing \(\Gamma(u)=1\), choose \(H\) exceeding all values of \(|u\cdot(x-y')+\epsilon f(p,y')|\) in a fixed source neighborhood, plus \(\delta\). Keep all evaluations \(a\cdot(z-p)\) in \([-H,H]\) unchanged and replace the remaining ones by the appropriate inequalities \(\geq H\) or \(\leq-H\). The old tilt is feasible. A minimum-norm solution has uniformly bounded norm because an independent subset of its active finite row system determines it through one of finitely many fixed pseudoinverses, with right sides bounded by \(H\). Every nonconstant smooth fiber integral is unchanged; saturated integrands remain identically zero or one. Thus the infimum is attained on a compact parameter set, and its own slab gives (1).

These arguments establish precisely the needed attainment and positivity premises. The separate actual body-minimum construction, normal-response formulas, and eventual quantitative OC payment remain obligations of the full smoothing route.

## 7. Uniform outward kernel

The same proof applies to the later primary choice
\(\Psi(t)=\min(1,\max(0,1+t))\), with
\(\psi=1_{(-1,0)}\). Although this kernel is not smooth pointwise, its integral \(T\) is continuously differentiable in \((a,u,b)\) whenever \(u\ne0\). Indeed both kink planes have zero mixed \(d\)-volume: each intersects a positive \(d\)-fiber in a hyperplane. Difference quotients are bounded on a compact neighborhood with \(u\ne0\), and converge away from those planes; dominated convergence gives the derivative formulas. Along a convergent parameter sequence the two limiting kink planes remain volume-null, so the derivatives are continuous by the same argument. The entire proof above uses precisely this \(C^1\) property, positivity of the slab mass, monotonicity, and finite saturation margins. It does not require pointwise smoothness of \(\Psi\).
